stories.title: EvilTokens: a phishing-as-a-service kit that steals Microsoft 365 tokens through device code phishing
stories.summary: EvilTokens is a phishing-as-a-service platform that appeared in February 2026 and abuses the OAuth device code flow. Microsoft says its campaigns compromised more than 12,000 inboxes in over 10,000 organizations. The victim is shown a real device code and sent to the genuine microsoft.com/devicelogin page, so the sign-in and MFA are done by the victim and the attacker receives the tokens without ever seeing a password. Stolen tokens were used to read and exfiltrate mail, create inbox rules and in some cases register a device to obtain a Primary Refresh Token. Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit coordinated a disruption of the infrastructure.

timeline.text: EvilTokens emerges as a phishing-as-a-service platform sold through Telegram. (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Microsoft tracks a related campaign that used automation platforms to start short-lived polling nodes running Node.js backend logic. (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Microsoft Threat Intelligence publishes its analysis and describes the coordinated disruption by the Digital Crimes Unit.

stories.rootCause: The device code flow lets a third party start a sign-in that the victim completes on a legitimate Microsoft page. Where Conditional Access does not block the flow, the attacker's polling script receives valid tokens after the victim signs in with MFA.
attacker: Developer and operator of the kit is tracked as Storm-2992; sold on Telegram for $1,500 plus $500 per month.

Lures by email (invoices, RFPs, shared files, password-expiry notices) with URLs, PDF or HTML attachments, behind fake CAPTCHA pages and multi-stage redirects on Vercel, Cloudflare Workers and AWS Lambda.
A background script requests a live device code, shows it with Copy Code and Continue buttons and polls the actor's /state endpoint every three to five seconds for up to 15 minutes.

After sign-in: Microsoft Graph reconnaissance, AI-assisted search for financial and executive mailboxes, wire-transfer and invoice keywords, malicious inbox rules, and device registration to obtain a Primary Refresh Token within about 10 minutes.
iocs: Hosting abused: .vercel.app, .workers.dev, AWS Lambda (named by Microsoft)
Microsoft lists no IP addresses or file hashes in this post

remediation.text: Block the device code flow with Conditional Access wherever possible; where Teams devices need it, scope the exception to the Teams device resource accounts and exclude the Device Registration Service resource.
Revoke refresh tokens with revokeSignInSessions for a suspected account and consider disabling it temporarily; access tokens can stay valid for up to an hour.
Require phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO, Authenticator with passkeys), enable sign-in risk policies and Continuous Access Evaluation, block legacy authentication.
Configure anti-phishing, Safe Links and ZAP, raise the Advanced Phishing Threshold to 2 or 3 and alert on suspicious inbox rule creation.

stories.title: Storm-3168 (JADEPUFFER): agentic destructive attack in Azure through compromised service principals
stories.summary: Microsoft investigated malicious Azure activity in one compromised tenant where two service principals were used: one for reconnaissance, the other for discovery, bulk deletion and credential collection. More than 150 destructive or credential-collection operations ran over 35 minutes, hitting storage accounts, a Key Vault, a Function App and an App Service plan; SQL deletions failed on an unsupported API version and some deletions were stopped by resource locks. Microsoft saw no ransom note and did not confirm data exfiltration. The actor is tracked as Storm-3168 and is associated with JADEPUFFER, which Sysdig reported in July 2026 as the first documented agentic ransomware operation.

timeline.text: Early June: the first service principal enumerates VMs, subscriptions and resources for about 15.5 hours; the second follows about 90 minutes later and later enumerates App Service configuration stores. (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Sysdig discovers JADEPUFFER (as reported by Microsoft). (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Microsoft Security Research publishes the analysis.

stories.rootCause: Initial access is unconfirmed. Microsoft found a client ID, secret and tenant ID posted in plaintext in a public GitHub issue by an employee and still visible in the edit history, but could not confirm that credential was used. The service principals held broad Azure RBAC roles (Contributor, Storage Account Contributor, SQL DB Contributor), which made the deletions possible.
attacker: Used existing Azure RBAC assignments of the two service principals; five unique tokens for the destructive principal, two active in the same 70-second window, assessed as automated.
User agent python-requests/2.34.2 and shared infrastructure for both principals.
Tried to delete Azure Site Recovery and Azure Backup protection locks (failed), then listed storage account keys 30+ times after the destruction.
iocs: 45.131.66[.]106 (App Service probing and malicious ARM requests)

remediation.text: Treat publicly exposed credentials as compromised even after the source is edited: rotate immediately and review historical use.
Apply least privilege to service principals through Azure RBAC and prefer mechanisms that reduce long-lived credentials.
Use resource locks and deletion protection, restrict access to backup and recovery resources and monitor attempts to change their protection.
Enable the Defender for Cloud plans for Resource Manager, Storage, Key Vault, App Service and Databases.

stories.title: Beyond source code: a self-service password reset on one account led to Azure DevOps pipelines and Kubernetes credentials
stories.summary: Microsoft's Detection and Response Team described an intrusion that began with a single user account taken over through self-service password reset (SSPR). The attacker registered their own authentication methods, then used legitimate admin tools and scripts to enumerate Azure DevOps repositories, projects and pipelines. A malicious pipeline harvested Kubernetes credentials (kubeconfig files); pipeline scripts were then changed to install the Atera remote management agent and the Chisel tunnelling tool. The page attributes the activity to Storm-3068 and gives no attack dates and no IOC values. The case shows how an identity weakness spreads when development platforms, pipelines and cloud infrastructure are tightly connected.

timeline.text: Microsoft publishes the incident-response write-up; the page gives no dates for the intrusion itself.

stories.rootCause: Initial access was abuse of self-service password reset on a user account, followed by registration of attacker-controlled authentication methods. The impact grew because the account's permissions reached Azure DevOps pipelines authorised for more than 50 resources. The page does not state a formal root cause.
attacker: Took over a user account through self-service password reset and registered their own authentication methods.
Enumerated Azure DevOps repositories, projects, pipelines and deployment environments with legitimate tools and scripts.
Created a pipeline that deployed a kube agent and collected kubeconfig files at scale.
Modified pipeline scripts to install the Atera agent and download the Chisel tunnelling utility; Chisel opened a reverse tunnel to an external IP address (value not published).
Committed seven stolen kubeconfig files to a repository.

remediation.text: Monitor password reset activity for unusual patterns, such as repeated attempts or activity across multiple users.
Limit privileged accounts' exposure to self-service password reset and require phishing-resistant MFA.
Require approvals for code changes, enforce branch protection and restrict direct commits to critical branches.
Control who can create, modify or run build and deployment pipelines; apply least privilege across identities, development platforms and cloud resources.
Review recently registered authentication methods on accounts that completed a password reset, and review Azure DevOps audit logs for new or changed pipelines.

stories.title: Sideloaded AppX package abuses Microsoft-signed web hosts to capture OAuth tokens (Huntress research)
stories.summary: Huntress researcher Andrew Schwartz showed that a sideloaded AppX package can use Microsoft-signed AppX web hosts such as WWAHost.exe to show a genuine Microsoft sign-in, complete MFA and hand the authorization code to attacker JavaScript, which exchanges it for access and refresh tokens. It is post-compromise: it needs code execution in the user's session and Developer Mode or an enterprise sideloading policy. It was proven end to end on Windows 11 24H2 against a test tenant with MFA. Huntress names no threat actor and discloses no attacker infrastructure, so this is a technique, not an observed campaign. The Entra sign-in looks like a normal Office sign-in with no risk flags.

timeline.text: Huntress publishes the research; the page gives no date for the testing itself.

stories.rootCause: A design issue in the shared WinRT activation layer: a sideloaded package with WindowsRuntimeAccess="all" in ContentUriRules gives remote JavaScript the WinRT surface, with no caller validation, and the legacy WebAuthenticationBroker is reachable from inside the host. Developer Mode or the AllowAllTrustedApps policy is the gating condition.
attacker: Registers a package with Add-AppxPackage -Register as a standard user; the manifest points ContentUriRules at an attacker server.
Calls WebAuthenticationBroker.authenticateAsync() with Microsoft Office's first-party client ID and the urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob redirect URI.
The user sees a real Microsoft login with no address bar and completes MFA.
Receives the authorization code through the broker callback, exchanges it and exfiltrates the access and refresh tokens.
iocs: User agent MSAppHost/3.0 (Edge/18) reaching non-Microsoft destinations (broker leg: MSAuthHost/1.0)
Add-AppxPackage -Register from paths outside C:\Program Files\WindowsApps

remediation.text: Deploy the Sigma proxy rule on user agent MSAppHost/3.0 with a Microsoft domain allow-list tuned to your environment.
Audit Developer Mode across the fleet and disable 'Allow all trusted apps to install' by GPO.
Require compliant or managed devices for token issuance with Conditional Access and pair with Token Protection where available.
Shorten refresh-token lifetimes and enable Continuous Access Evaluation.

links.text: OAuth Token Theft Through Microsoft's Front Door
